## Preface to «Inevitable Escape»

Issue 1193 – 4 September 2008
Mihan Rusta

Mahnaz Matin

Sirous Javidi

Nasser Mohajer

The initial idea for this volume was proposed by Mihan Rusta. In Farvardin 1384 / April 2005, she came to Paris to say to us: let us join hands and write down the whys and wherefores of how our generation left behind loved ones and homeland, and publish it in book form — for a generation whose bond with our generation has been severed: both those who have lived these past twenty-odd years inside Iran, grown up under the suffocating repression of the Islamic Republic, and possess no comprehensive grasp of bygone days; and those who have grown up outside Iran and ask today: how did it come about that we were severed from our soil and roots and carried off in all directions like violets? Mihan’s conversations with Mahnaz Matin, Sirous Javidi, and Nasser Mohajer, conducted at first one by one, culminated in a collective dialogue amongst the four of us. In the course of this dialogue, we unpacked the initial idea, examined several of its dimensions, and declared our readiness to advance the work. Thus, we made Mihan’s idea our own.

Upon Mihan’s return to Berlin, and during several Paltalk discussions that we organised amongst ourselves in May and June, that initial idea evolved into a preliminary working plan. We named the project "Recounting Memories of Escape and Life in Exile"; we committed it to paper in July 2005 and disseminated it through several channels: first through our wide network of friendships and acquaintances, then on several websites, and finally in a periodical. After a while, we made minor revisions to the initial text and called upon our exiled and émigré compatriots «to send a summary of their outline or text to our email address by the end of October 2005». We articulated the rationale of our project as follows:

«Flight and life in exile represent an important experience in the history of Iran’s political and social struggles. Recording this experience and transmitting it to future generations is of particular importance. For this very reason, we have placed the collection and rewriting of these experiences on our agenda, so that we may do our part to prevent this chapter of our country’s history from falling into oblivion.

The timeframe we have set for this collection is the years 1360 to 1365 (1981–1986) — precisely those years during which figures from the left-wing and democratic spectrum were compelled on a massive scale to leave Iran. We have chosen this period because we possess greater knowledge of its complexities and details.»

Several months passed and no more than a handful of texts reached us, and even those were the fruit of our network of friendships and acquaintances. From the outset, we more or less knew that most of the book’s contributions would come through that channel. Our experience in cultural and journalistic work amongst exiled and émigré Iranians, as well as our familiarity with the prevailing culture within this community, left no room for hesitation: we had to approach individuals directly and ask them to write down their recollections or recount them to us. Nevertheless, we resolved to entrust the call for contributions once more to several independent-minded websites so as to step beyond the circle of direct and indirect friendships and acquaintances. This time too, we did not obtain what we sought. Only a few acquaintances contacted us, enquired briefly about our working plan, and shared a little of the story of their own escape — without any firm commitment.

From that point onwards, the discussions within our four-person circle took on a new dimension. Which experiences ought we to record in this volume? Upon which aspects of “departing from the soil” do we wish to dwell? From the vast multitude of exiled and émigré Iranians, whom should we select? And on the basis of what criteria?

Dialogue around these questions brought about an expansion of the circle of potential contributors to this book: several million Iranians live outside Iran. Not all of them were political activists, nor did all leave their homeland for that reason. Even during that very period of 1360–1365 (1981–1986), which was fundamentally the period of flight for supporters of the Bahman 1357 (February 1979) Revolution and radical opponents of the Islamic Republic, many emigrated from Iran because the Islamic Republic utterly denied their identity and basic rights, and they refused to submit to Sharia laws and the ideological policies of the regime, and were therefore subjected to continuous harassment and persecution by the rulers. For example: Baha'is, Jews, Armenians and Assyrians, Zoroastrians, Kurds, dissidents, nonconformists, cultural figures and journalists, artists, lawyers, academics, teachers, workers, civil servants, homosexuals, deserters from the fronts of the war with Iraq, “purged” military personnel, and others… We needed to include one or more examples from these social groups alongside political activists — from every circle and current — so that the work would achieve comprehensiveness.

We compiled a list of individuals’ names as well as religious, professional, and political groups. Some of them we knew closely; some from afar; and some we did not know at all. We divided the names amongst ourselves and reached out. Empathy and willingness to cooperate were widespread. Our request was that individual narratives be recounted within the social and political context prevailing during their final months of life in Iran; that the reason or set of reasons that led to leaving the homeland be clearly set forth; that the route taken, the manner of crossing the border, and the hardships of the journey be depicted; and that the nature of the temporary stay in the neighbouring country, as well as the manner of reaching the final destination, be described. Several preferred to tell the story of their escape in response to our questions. Two individuals did not say “no” to us, yet deferred the task indefinitely and ultimately deprived the reader of their account.

Our difficulty, however, lay in finding Baha'i, Jewish, Christian, and Zoroastrian compatriots who were willing and able to give voice to what had befallen — and continues to befall — themselves and their co-religionists. Those whom we knew had long since abandoned the religion and traditions of their ancestors, and amongst their own relatives and kin they knew few who wished or were able to undertake such a task. Guidance from them and from others who had acquaintances amongst adherents of these faiths proved of little avail, and the effort led to semi-official — and in one instance official — contacts with the directors of their community institutions in various cities of America and Europe, without any result. Thus we turned once more to our friends and friends of friends, asking them to commit to paper the experience they had lived as a Christian, a Jew, or a left-wing Baha'i in Islamic Iran. Here it is fitting to thank Houman Azarkolah. We had asked him to introduce us to one of the women artists of pre-revolutionary theatre and cinema living in self-imposed exile, and he spoke to us of Farzaneh Ta'idi, whom they had tormented and whose life they had consumed both because of her acting career and because of her Baha'i background. And it is a pity that despite all our efforts, we were unable to bring any Zoroastrian on board to portray a glimpse of the persecution, discrimination, and humiliation inflicted upon adherents of this ancient Iranian faith — which has caused their widespread emigration, especially to North America.

Our other difficulty was persuading former or current supporters of the People's Mojahedin Organisation of Iran to record the account of their journey in this volume. Amongst the former Mojahedin whom we knew, for reasons we could not fathom, no one was ready to speak. We shared this difficulty with Iraj Mesdaghi, and after some time he introduced us to Mina Entezari, who warmly and openly accepted our proposal. We owe our access to her story to Iraj Mesdaghi. Mina’s account shook us so deeply that we altered the timeframe established in our initial plan and extended its scope to the end of the 1360s (1980s). Meanwhile, Nasser Pakdaman informed us of the travelogue of Jamshid Golmakani — today’s documentary filmmaker and yesterday’s journalist — written shortly after his departure from Iran and arrival in France. We are grateful to him for enriching this volume with so pure a testimony regarding the hardships of crossing the Pakistani border with empty hands, and for capturing the spirit and atmosphere of the young people who made their way through that route to Spain.

The effort to bring the work to completion as thoroughly as possible took considerable time and came at the cost of a long wait for publication amongst those colleagues who delivered their texts to us promptly. Here we must name Nahid Nosrat, who was the very first person to write her narrative and entrust it to us. We deeply appreciate her patience, as well as the patience of Asad Seif and Shadi Samand.

The first three texts we received bore pseudonyms and pen-name signatures. We knew all three authors closely, as well as their considerations and concerns. We had no objection to pseudonyms. We have held, and continue to hold, the conviction that so long as tyranny endures, pseudonyms will also remain in use. The real issue has been the improper abuse of this protective shield: namely, refusing to accept responsibility for one’s own words and deeds, and violating the dignity of others under the cover of an anonymous name. And since we regarded the writings in this volume as a form of intimate self-reflection (hadith-e nafs) — an inward gaze upon oneself and a voicing of one’s own life history — we insisted solely upon the principle of including texts, whether under a pseudonym or under a legal birth-certificate name, whose author we knew and regarding the authenticity of whose narrative we harboured no doubt.

We read the texts carefully. Whenever a gap came to our notice or greater precision and clarification seemed necessary, we discussed it with the author. Most important of all was verifying the chronology of political, social, and cultural events and the sequence of what came before and after. The passage of some two decades had subjected memories to a certain degree of forgetfulness. We took it upon ourselves to mend the frailty of memory with the help of newspapers, chronologies, periodicals, pamphlets, leaflets, and even eyewitnesses, and by supplying short and at times extensive footnotes as well as appendices, to provide the socio-political context and primary backdrop of events. We applied this same method in the interviews as well, with the unstinting assistance of Banafsheh Masoudi, Bahman Siavoshan, and our friends at the Archive of Iranian Documents and Research – Berlin.

In two cases, with the interviewee’s permission, we shaped the interview into a continuous narrative text — principally because the questions themselves did not contain particular information. Yet with everyone we sat down to interview, we strove beforehand to familiarise ourselves with the trajectory of their social life and to have read the most important documents and records relating to their profession and occupation. The difficulty of this working method lay in the repeated back-and-forth of the text between the author and the editorial circle; its reward was the forging of a link between the narrators’ lives and certain trends, events, and institutions that shaped the history of that period, as well as their shared destiny with the professional associations, political organisations, and democratic societies that blossomed during the "Spring of Freedom" and withered in the sweeping repression following 30 Khordad 1360 (20 June 1981).

When we reached the midpoint of our work, the artistic and technical dimensions of publishing the book came into prominence. We intended, through drawings and paintings, to capture moments of what had befallen those who fled their homeland. We believed that this approach would embody the spirit of relationships, events, and confrontations, and thereby keep alive the contexts and manifestations of “tearing oneself away from one’s very soul” through the visual arts. Above all, however, we had to devise a solution for the book’s cover. In consultation with Amir Houshang Keshavarz Sadr, Ariou Mashayekhi was mentioned; immediately, he picked up the telephone, dialled Ariou’s number, spoke a few sentences about the book and its editors, and then called Nasser Mohajer to speak with Ariou. In order to design the book’s cover, Ariou asked us to send him a selection of the articles and interviews in our possession. We sent them. The narratives sank deep into his soul, and he set down the essence of each one — just as he perceived it — upon paper and canvas:

«I could not depict the execution of the Ka'bi sisters in Kurdistan in any other way. I could not place headscarves upon their heads. I removed their headscarves to show their nobility and freedom of spirit. Out of fidelity to the ethical code of their profession — which was nursing — they had defended the rights of their patient, even though he was their enemy. Unconsciously, I draped a colourful shawl around their necks. Kurdistan is full of colour. I wanted to set colour, which symbolises life, against black, which symbolises death. I could not bring myself to close their eyes. Yet because of the final conversation they had with one another, I closed their eyes. The shooting of these two sisters was a shooting aimed at Kurdistan itself.» Or: «In Abbas Keyghobadi’s narrative, what pained me deeply was a scene when Abbas was in prison and asked to be taken to the lavatory. He is led to a cell that has a toilet, into which a father and his four- or five-year-old boy had been thrown. The boy is terrified. He thinks Abbas is a Revolutionary Guard who has come to take his father back to the torture chamber. Seeing the terrified face of the boy and the slow movement of a father’s hand — a father who, from the severity of torture, no longer had any strength left — Abbas completely forgets that he had needed the lavatory. Turning to the little boy, he says: “Do not be afraid, little nephew (amoo-jan), I am just like your dad!” This scene had the exact same impact upon me as the scene of the execution of the two Ka'bi sisters. The essence of both episodes is their killing and human dignity — the killing of humanity itself.» Or: «In Taqi Tam’s narrative, he speaks of his friend Behrouz Nabet, who was always asking questions and seeking new theories. I do not know why, when I was reading the account of his execution, the scene came before my eyes of Behrouz using the last minutes of his life to deliver a speech — and in this speech, instead of chanting slogans against his enemies, he speaks of his dreams for a free Iran and of everyone having freedom of choice.»

Gradually, Ariou became one of the firm pillars and foundations of this work. We owe our friendship and collaboration with this humanist artist to Amir Houshang Keshavarz Sadr. Together with a friend who prefers to remain unnamed, they endowed this book with a form and appearance worthy of its content and theme.

From the very start of our work, we wished that one of the narratives of inevitable escape might appear in the language of poetry. Yet we had no clear idea for assembling a selection of narratives of leaving the homeland composed in verse. It was in the course of our work and research into exile literature that we realised how numerous are the poets of our homeland who have tasted exile and left behind a rich legacy — both in classical poetry and in modern poetry, which remains to this day the most effective medium for expressing the feelings and thoughts of us Iranians. Nor could it have been otherwise. A people repeatedly exposed to assaults by both foreigner and compatriot, endowed with a rich tradition of struggle against global predators and tyrants, and repeatedly forced to uproot themselves from the nest, endure wandering, and settle beneath “the sky of anywhere whatsoever”, could not fail to recount their feelings, sights, and lived experiences in the language of poetry:

Listen to the reed as it tells its tale / Complaining of separations

O Sa'di, though love of the homeland be a true saying / One cannot die in hardship merely because I was born there

I did not surrender my home to another / Fate drove me out of my house

The ominous clamour of jackals / The incessant cawing of crows wore you down

Alas! When I packed my belongings and departed from a homeland that was becoming the killer of either my life or my ideal…

Come, let us gather provisions for the journey / And set foot upon the road… Where? Wherever it may lead

Bon voyage! Yet, for friendship’s sake, by God / When you have passed safely through this desert of terror / To the blossoms, to the rain / Convey our greetings

Whoever remains far from their origin / Seeks once more the time of reunion
*

Here, one final day, from the mountain crest, like the sun / I shall sing the song of victory / And I know / You shall one day return.

We have gathered in this volume a bouquet from the treasury of exile poems relating to the Islamic Republic — not merely to adorn the work, but because certain narratives of escape have been recounted wholly in the language of poetry. And alas that we could not, and it did not prove possible to, gather more accounts in verse. It must also be noted that amongst the pieces we selected, only Shafi'i Kadkani’s “Safar be Kheyr” (“Bon Voyage”), which is a meditation upon the category of inevitable escape, was composed during the reign of Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi.

We were unable to include an example from every social and political group in this volume. Contrary to the plan we had laid out, we did not find certain examples; others we found only when it had already grown far too late. Three individuals said half-way through — and did not say — that they could not commit their story to pen. Behrouz Javidi, whose story of escape was to appear in this book, passed away from amongst us — a hundred pities — in Tir 1385 / July 2006. One person, at the very moment when the final edited version of their interview with us was ready for print, did not wish to expose the horrifying experience they had lived to public judgement; and because we did not wish to add to their suffering, we refrained from including a text that would have enhanced the comprehensiveness of this volume. Let us state right here that we set aside none of the narratives that reached us.

We are aware that several of the articles and interviews included in this volume are unfinished stories. We did not deem it right to compel the narrators to say more than they themselves wished or were currently able to say. And we are aware that, even though more than two decades have passed since the second wave of inevitable escape, the untold stories remain legion. And we are likewise aware that the wounds are still open, the pains remain unhealed, and language is incapable of expressing them. Our hope, however, is that we have paved just a small part of the ground for the retelling of other narratives — which are countless — so that eventually the severed threads of the reality of what has befallen our homeland and our people may be woven together, and a part of the whole of a historical period may be reconstructed, lest oblivion prevail and tragedy repeat itself.

And our final word is that "Inevitable Escape" was, in the truest sense of the word, a collective endeavour. The assistance of Kourosh Amjadi, Leila Aslani, Golrokh Jahangiri, Azar Habib, Mahnoush Dalaei, Asad Seif, Mitra Gousheh, Shohreh Mahmoud, Simin Nassiri, and Hamid Nozari is unforgettable. We are especially grateful to Farideh Zebarjad and Baqer Mortazavi, who stood by us from the beginning of the work to its end, as well as to Abbas Khodagholi. Finally, we must name the Association of Iranian Political Refugees in Berlin and Umverteilen Stiftung für solidarische Welt AG Frauen, of whom the former strove within its capacity to lend us a helping hand and the latter came to our aid.

Nazanin Paydar
Journalist

"Inevitable Escape" is the title of a two-volume book comprising thirty narratives of escape from Iran in the 1980s (the Iranian decade of the 1360s), recently released onto the Persian book market in Europe and America by Nashr-e Noghteh in Paris.
During the 1980s (1360s), a large number of activists affiliated with left-wing and democratic thought left Iran; yet the reasons why and the manner in which they departed from Iran remain matters about which today’s generation, nearly three decades after that period, still knows very little.

According to what is stated in the preface to "Inevitable Escape", the editors’ aim in compiling this book is an endeavour to record the reasons for this widespread flight and to provide information to today’s generation.

In books published inside Iran, only passing references have been made to the clashes amongst various political groups and the social crises of the 1980s (1360s). Amongst them, certain clerics, such as Ayatollah Khalkhali, in their memoirs have looked at these years only selectively and from their own particular vantage point.

Those who have recounted their memories and reasons for fleeing Iran in "Inevitable Escape" are mostly socio-political activists, artists, writers, and researchers, each of whom, in their narrative spanning from the years of the revolution to the mid-1980s (mid-1360s), presents a picture of Iran’s political, social, and cultural conditions in light of the scope of their professional and political relationships and activities rooted in their interests and expertise.

In particular, some of these memoirs examine the nature and scope of the activities of various institutions and associations between 1978 and 1981 (1357–1360) — institutions such as the Bar Association, the Independent Teachers’ Association, and the Oil Workers’ Syndicate, which were established in the years preceding the revolution or immediately thereafter.

"Spoken and Unspoken Dimensions"

In "Inevitable Escape", in addition to presenting the memoirs of a large number of political and social activists, the escape narratives of those who were subjected to pressures by the government of the time on account of their ethnic, religious, and confessional identity are also included.

For example, "Farzaneh Ta'idi", a cinema and theatre actress, in recounting her memories speaks both of the hardships faced by Baha'is at that juncture and of the difficulties that beset her as an established veteran actress.

The book was compiled, edited, and curated by four researchers: "Mihan Rusta", "Mahnaz Matin", "Sirous Javidi", and "Nasser Mohajer".

Nasser Mohajer, who has for years been engaged in research on prisons and political prisoners, speaking of previous efforts to collect accounts of Iranians fleeing the country and noting that a number of prison memoirs have also touched upon this subject, albeit briefly, explains: "Nearly ten years ago, Ms Kian Katouzian, the wife of Mr Ali-Asghar Haj-Seyyed-Javadi, published a book on this topic entitled From Dawn to Dusk (Az Sepideh ta Sham), which recounts her own escape and that of her two daughters from Iran to France. This book is not solely an account of escape; it is also a kind of political memoir encompassing a description of the political activities of the Haj-Seyyed-Javadis from the eve of the revolution until Khordad 1360 (June 1981)."

Mr Mohajer continues: "Apart from this book and the works Akbar Sardouzami has produced in this field — including the book Wandering Through Unfamiliar Backstreets — I can name the memoirs of several veteran Tudeh Party members: From Anzali to Dushanbe by Mohammad Rouzegar, From the Military Organisation of the Tudeh Party to the Detention Camps of Siberia by Fereydoun Pishvapour, and most recently, The Years Left Behind by M. A. Sarabi. Several political prisoners of the 1980s (1360s) have also written their prison recollections in this vein, including Hassan Darvish, who devoted a considerable portion of his book, The Tale Is Still Remembered, to why and how he fled Iran."

.
In those very first years after leaving Iran, around 1984–85, Nasser Mohajer compiled the escape narrative of Ms "Vida Hajebi Tabrizi", author of the book "Dad-e Bidad" ("A Cry Against Injustice"), from Tehran to Kurdistan, Turkey, and thence to Europe, which was printed in booklet form.

He says: "Of course, at that time I had not yet realised that this single instance of inevitable escape and the great exodus was a page in the socio-political history of Islamic Iran that needed to be recorded and studied by future generations. Undoubtedly, before then, many had written the story of being uprooted, of crossing the desert of terror, and of alighting in foreign lands, and these had been circulated to a limited extent. The difficulty of publishing abroad must not be underestimated. Many of the books and booklets printed in one country — and even in one city — never reach other cities and countries."

With the passage of time, the retelling of many memories loses somewhat of its requisite precision, and it is precisely this that makes repeated consultation of newspapers and informational sources from the period in question indispensable for the researcher.

This task becomes all the more arduous in compiling a book like "Inevitable Escape" given that the documents and publications of many political organisations and parties were destroyed in the 1980s (1360s).

Nevertheless, the editors of "Inevitable Escape" state that in order to raise the level of accuracy of the memoirs published in this book, they strove to gain access to those sources. Nasser Mohajer says: "Let us bear in mind that more than twenty years have passed since the events that the narrators sat down to recount, and willy-nilly this settles the dust of forgetfulness over certain matters and brings errors of memory regarding others."

Mr Mohajer adds: "More generally, as you know, in writing and recounting memoirs, certain facets of events are spoken while other facets remain unspoken; nor is this treatment of events necessarily deliberate. Therefore, from the very outset, we resolved to apply recognised mechanisms for verifying dates and events: namely, consulting newspapers, partisan and non-partisan weeklies, communiqués and declarations, chronicles, and making enquiries of those who had participated directly or indirectly in an episode."

.
The footnotes to the memoirs published in this book constitute yet another of its sections.

Mr Mohajer says: "After receiving the first text, we realised it was necessary to write a few lines about the executed individuals whom the author had mentioned, so that someone who lost their life in the struggle for people to attain a better life would not remain unknown. We then noticed that at certain points and on certain subjects the author made only a passing reference and moved on. From then on, the work of footnoting became more serious. We decided to introduce some of the major events of the revolution — such as the events in Kurdistan, the closure of the newspaper Ayandegan, and the march that followed it — in several lines for the reader who does not remember those events or has not read much about them."

Beyond Memoir-Writing

In Nasser Mohajer’s view, scrupulous care in accurately recounting what was heard and seen, refraining from embellishing events and trends, avoiding hero-worship and fictionalisation, refraining from imposing personal bias in reporting — belittling or wholly omitting whomever and whatever we dislike while magnifying and giving prominence to whomever and whatever we favour — distinguishing the exception from the rule, adhering to reality, and maintaining fidelity in narration are among the principles that must be observed in memoir-writing.

Having written several books and articles to date on the prisons of the 1980s (1360s) — including compiling in "The Prison Book" ("Ketab-e Zendan") a collection of memoirs and articles by several former political prisoners — he says: "In most cases where a memoirist has placed themselves in the position of a historian or a fiction writer, historical reality has been mutilated and has more or less lost its value. In Inevitable Escape, we have striven not to step beyond the bounds of memoir-writing."

Some of the memoirs published in "Inevitable Escape" are presented in the form of dialogues, namely: Houshang Keshavarz Sadr (anthropologist and researcher), Ali Shahendeh (former lawyer), Farzaneh Ta'idi (Iranian theatre and cinema actress), Fatemeh Saeedi (political activist), Hamid Ahmadi (researcher on the history of the Left), Raouf Ka'bi (political activist), Baqer Momeni (writer and researcher of contemporary history), and Hassan Makaremi (writer).

Other memoirists in the book: Haideh Daragahi (former assistant professor at the University of Tehran, political and women’s rights activist), Reza Marzban (journalist), Nahid Nosrat (political activist), Ozra Bani-Sadr (wife of Abolhassan Bani-Sadr), Mina Entezari (political activist), Shadi Samand (filmmaker), Louise Baghramian (political activist), Yadollah Khosrowshahi (activist in Iran’s trade-union and labour movement), Jamshid Golmakani (documentary filmmaker), Ahmad Asadi (political activist), Nasser Mohajer (writer and researcher), Leila Aslani (political activist), Mitra Sadat (political activist), Mahnaz Matin (women’s rights activist and researcher), Sirous Javid (political activist), Roya Hakakian (writer and poet), Haideh Torabi (theatre actress), Nassim Khaksar (fiction writer), Taqi Tam (political activist), Sorour Ali-Mohammadi (political activist), Asad Seif (writer and researcher), Akbar Sardouzami (fiction writer), Saba Farnoud (physician), Abbas Keyghobadi (political activist), and Mohsen Yalfani (playwright).

The thirty narrators of "Inevitable Escape" hold diverse positions in terms of social, specialist, and professional standing, and have therefore looked from different angles at one of the most critical decades in contemporary Iranian history.
